explanation: Present value translates future cash into today's equivalent at a selected discount rate. Future value grows today's cash forward at a compounding rate. These are inverse operations when rates, timing and conventions match.

For one future amount, PV = FV/(1 + r)^n and FV = PV(1 + r)^n. The rate reflects the valuation purpose and relevant risk; using a convenient rate without justification can reverse the investment decision.

types.name: Future value
types.explanation: Accumulated value at a future date.

types.name: Single amount versus stream
types.explanation: One receipt versus several separately dated payments.

workedCase.setup: Assume ₹121 lakh will be received in two years and the appropriate annual rate is 10%.
workedCase.result: Discounting and compounding reconcile under identical assumptions.
workedCase.interpretation: A riskier promise may require a different valuation approach or rate; the arithmetic alone does not establish its certainty.

analysis: Draw the date of each amount.
Match rate to currency and risk.
Check that forward and backward calculations reconcile.

explanation: Compounding moves cash forward; discounting moves it backward. The same percentage produces asymmetric monetary changes because each operation uses a different base. Financial analysis must keep the valuation date consistent before adding cash flows.
Discounting is not subtracting interest linearly from the future amount. At a positive rate, a later receipt is worth less today, and a higher discount rate lowers its present value.

types.name: Multi-period discounting
types.explanation: Apply the full number of periods.

workedCase.setup: At 10%, ₹100 grows to ₹110 after one year.
steps: Discount ₹110 by dividing by 1.10 to recover ₹100.
Subtracting 10% of ₹110 instead gives ₹99, which is incorrect for this reversal.
At 20%, the same ₹110 future receipt has PV ₹91.67.
workedCase.result: The denominator, not a simple subtraction, reverses compounding.
workedCase.interpretation: All compared opportunities need a common valuation date and compatible treatment of distributions and risk.

analysis: Write the growth factor explicitly.
Keep valuation dates consistent.
Check rate and period conventions.

explanation: A discount factor is the present value of one unit paid at a specified future date. With a flat annual rate, DF(t) = 1/(1 + r)^t. A cash-flow timeline places every receipt and payment at its actual date, preventing accidental early or late discounting.
Different maturities can have different discount factors from a yield curve. A flat-rate classroom model is a simplification, not a requirement that every future payment share one rate.

workedCase.setup: A project costs ₹100 today and pays ₹60 at each of the next two year-ends. Use 10%.
workedCase.result: The initial outlay is not discounted again.
workedCase.interpretation: Moving a receipt one year earlier changes value even when total undiscounted receipts remain ₹120.

analysis: Label time zero.
Assign each cash flow a date.
Use the appropriate discount factor for that date.

explanation: An ordinary annuity pays an equal amount at each period-end. An annuity due pays at each period-start, so every payment arrives one period earlier. For positive rates, the due annuity has higher present value because less waiting is required.
Ordinary PV = payment × [1 − (1 + r)^−n]/r. Annuity-due PV is the ordinary value multiplied by (1 + r), assuming otherwise identical dates and rate conventions.

types.name: Deferred annuity
types.explanation: Equal payments starting after an additional delay.

workedCase.setup: Receive ₹10 annually for three years at 10%, comparing year-ends 1–3 with beginnings 0–2.
steps: The due value equals ₹24.87 × 1.10, subject to rounding.
workedCase.result: Earlier timing adds about ₹2.49 of present value.
workedCase.interpretation: Real leases and savings plans may have irregular dates or escalation, requiring explicit timelines instead of the equal-payment formula.

analysis: Identify the first payment date.
Count payments, not just years.
Use explicit flows when amounts or dates vary.

explanation: A growing annuity is a finite stream whose payments grow at a constant rate. With first payment C1 at year one, PV = C1/(r − g) × [1 − ((1 + g)/(1 + r))^n] when r differs from g.

The first-payment convention matters: applying growth twice overstates cash flows. If r equals g, calculate the limit or sum individual payments rather than dividing by zero. Finite streams need not satisfy the perpetual-growth restriction in the same way.

types.name: Growing annuity
types.explanation: Payments rise at a fixed rate.

types.name: Declining annuity
types.explanation: Payments fall at a fixed rate.

workedCase.setup: First payment is ₹10 lakh, growth 5%, discount rate 10%, and there are three year-end receipts.
workedCase.result: Growth affects payment amounts; discounting separately affects their present value.
workedCase.interpretation: A constant growth assumption may poorly fit salary increases or business cycles; an explicit schedule is safer when patterns change.

analysis: Specify C1 rather than an ambiguous current payment.
Check finite horizon and growth rate.
Verify the formula against a short explicit timeline.

explanation: A perpetuity pays indefinitely. A level perpetuity with first payment next period has PV = C1/r. A growing perpetuity has PV = C1/(r − g) only when r exceeds g under the constant-growth model.

The value is sensitive to a small gap between r and g. A terminal value in DCF is measured at the end of the forecast period and must still be discounted to today. Perpetuity does not mean the company is immune to competition or reinvestment needs.

types.name: Level perpetuity
types.explanation: Constant payments without a final date.

types.name: Growing perpetuity
types.explanation: Constant-rate growth forever under model assumptions.

types.name: Deferred perpetuity
types.explanation: First payment begins after an additional delay.

workedCase.setup: Assume next-year distributable cash is ₹10 lakh, r = 10% and g = 3%.
steps: At r = g, the finite formula is invalid because the infinite series does not converge.
workedCase.result: A one-point growth change materially changes value.
workedCase.interpretation: Sustainable growth normally requires reinvestment; do not increase distributable cash growth without modelling its economic cost.

analysis: Confirm r exceeds g.
Use the next-period cash flow.
Stress-test the rate-growth gap and reinvestment assumptions.

explanation: Uneven cash flows have different amounts or dates and should be valued individually. Sum each payment multiplied by its own discount factor. An annuity shortcut is inappropriate unless the stream actually fits its payment pattern.

For irregular calendar dates, date-based conventions may be needed rather than treating all periods as identical. Multiple changes of cash-flow sign can also complicate IRR and create several or no meaningful roots.

types.name: Mixed-sign flows
types.explanation: Receipts and additional investments over time.

workedCase.setup: A project costs ₹100 lakh now, pays ₹30 in year one and ₹90 in year two. Use 10%.
workedCase.result: A small positive NPV depends on the actual payment sequence.
workedCase.interpretation: A ₹90 first receipt and ₹30 second receipt would have higher value despite identical total proceeds.

analysis: List every dated payment.
Discount separately before summing.
Check timing and sign changes.

explanation: A nominal annual rate with m compounding periods has periodic rate j/m under that quotation convention. The effective annual rate is (1 + j/m)^m − 1. Continuous compounding uses an annual growth factor e^j.

The word nominal here describes a rate quotation; it can also mean unadjusted for inflation in another context. State which meaning is intended. Product fees and day-count conventions can make realised yields differ from a simple quoted rate.

types.name: Effective annual rate
types.explanation: Actual one-year growth under the specified periodic convention.

workedCase.setup: A deposit quotes 12% nominal annual interest compounded monthly.
workedCase.result: The annual effective rate exceeds the 12% nominal quote.
workedCase.interpretation: Comparing this product with a 12.5% effective quote requires matching conventions and accounting for fees and credit risk.

analysis: Read the quote convention.
Convert to a common effective period.
Include fees and day-count differences where relevant.

explanation: Nominal rates include the effect of changing price levels; real rates measure purchasing-power growth. The exact relationship is 1 + nominal return = (1 + real return)(1 + inflation). Subtracting inflation is an approximation that becomes less accurate at larger rates.
Real cash flows should be discounted at a consistent real rate; nominal cash flows at a consistent nominal rate. Mixing them can double-count or omit inflation.

types.name: Expected versus realised inflation
types.explanation: Forecast used in planning versus actual price change.

workedCase.setup: An investment returns 10% while the relevant price index rises 6%.
steps: Real return ≈ 3.77%, versus the 4% subtraction approximation.
workedCase.result: A money gain of 10% is a smaller purchasing-power gain.
workedCase.interpretation: Personal inflation can differ from a broad index because spending baskets differ; the assumed inflation measure should fit the objective.

analysis: Match real flows with real rates.
Identify the inflation index and horizon.
Distinguish expected and realised purchasing-power outcomes.

explanation: Amortisation repays a loan through payments containing interest and principal. For a fully amortising fixed-rate loan, payment = P × r/[1 − (1 + r)^−n], using the payment-period rate. Interest is charged on outstanding principal, so its share of a level payment declines over time.
A balloon loan leaves principal due at maturity; interest-only payments do not amortise the balance. Fees, floating rates, prepayment and payment dates can change actual schedules.

types.name: Fully amortising
types.explanation: Principal reaches zero through scheduled payments.

workedCase.setup: Borrow ₹100 lakh at 10% annually, repaid through two equal year-end payments.
steps: Year-one interest is ₹10; principal repayment is ₹47.62; balance is ₹52.38.
Year-two interest is about ₹5.24; remaining principal is repaid by the second payment.
workedCase.result: A constant payment contains changing interest and principal shares.
workedCase.interpretation: The annual example uses simplified dates; a monthly EMI schedule must use monthly rates and payment counts.

analysis: Separate interest from principal.
Reconcile opening and closing debt.
Read reset, fee and prepayment terms.

explanation: A sinking fund accumulates cash for a future obligation. Equal end-period contributions have FV = contribution × [(1 + r)^n − 1]/r. Beginning-period contributions earn one extra period of return.

The required contribution depends on target date, existing savings, expected return and uncertainty. A deterministic savings formula does not guarantee a risky portfolio will reach the target; liability matching and contingency contributions may be needed.

types.name: End-period saving
types.explanation: Each contribution starts earning after period-end.

types.name: Existing lump sum
types.explanation: Opening savings compound alongside new contributions.

workedCase.setup: Save ₹100 at each of two year-ends at 10% annually.
steps: The first contribution grows for one year to ₹110.
The second contribution arrives at the target date and remains ₹100.
workedCase.result: Two beginning-year contributions instead accumulate ₹231 at year two.
workedCase.interpretation: The difference reflects timing, not a higher return rate; changing contribution dates requires a different timeline.

analysis: Define the target date and amount.
Include existing savings separately.
Stress-test returns and contribution interruptions.

explanation: NPV is the present value of all incremental project cash flows, including the initial outlay. Positive NPV means the project is expected to exceed the required compensation for risk and timing under the model. It measures value in currency rather than a percentage return.

Use after-tax incremental cash flows, opportunity costs and working-capital effects where relevant. Financing costs should not be counted twice through both project cash flows and a financing-inclusive discount rate.

types.name: Independent project
types.explanation: Accept based on value and constraints.

types.name: Constrained investment
types.explanation: Consider funding and operational limitations alongside NPV.

workedCase.setup: Pay ₹100 today and receive ₹110 in one year; required return is 10%.
steps: At a purchase cost of ₹95, NPV becomes ₹5.
workedCase.result: Zero NPV earns exactly the required return under the assumptions.
workedCase.interpretation: It is not zero accounting profit; positive expected earnings may simply compensate for the capital committed.

analysis: Use incremental cash flows.
Apply an appropriate discount rate.
Test assumptions and alternative uses of capital.

explanation: IRR is a discount rate making NPV zero. It is intuitive for conventional investments but can misrank projects with different scale or timing. Multiple sign changes can create multiple IRRs, while some streams have no useful IRR.

MIRR separates a financing rate for negative flows and reinvestment rate for positive flows. It provides one defined compound rate under its conventions, but remains a rate metric; value-maximising comparisons should still examine NPV.

types.name: MIRR
types.explanation: Rate connecting financed outflows with reinvested inflows.

workedCase.setup: Project A costs ₹100 and pays ₹130 next year; B costs ₹1,000 and pays ₹1,200. Use a 10% hurdle.
steps: IRRs are 30% for A and 20% for B.
workedCase.result: The higher IRR project creates less absolute value.
workedCase.interpretation: If funding is limited or projects cannot be scaled, evaluate the actual feasible choices rather than ranking by one metric.

analysis: Inspect cash-flow signs.
Compare NPV at the relevant hurdle.
State MIRR finance and reinvestment rates.

explanation: Money-weighted return reflects the size and timing of external contributions and withdrawals, usually through an IRR calculation. Time-weighted return divides the history at external flows and compounds subperiod returns, reducing the effect of the investor's flow timing.

Use money-weighted performance for the experience of invested money and time-weighted performance for evaluating a manager who does not control external flows. Accurate valuation at flow dates is important.

types.name: External flow
types.explanation: Contribution or withdrawal separated from investment earnings.

workedCase.setup: An account starts at ₹100, rises 10% to ₹110, receives ₹100 new contribution, then falls 10% to ₹189.
workedCase.result: The account's currency gain or loss is not its time-weighted return.
workedCase.interpretation: A money-weighted calculation must include the dated ₹100 contribution; it will reflect that more money was exposed during the losing period.

analysis: Separate external flows from returns.
Value the account at flow boundaries.
Select the metric for the evaluation purpose.

explanation: Valuation requires consistency among cash-flow frequency, currency, inflation treatment and discount rate. Monthly payments cannot be discounted as if they were annual payments. Foreign-currency flows need either a coherent currency-specific discounting approach or consistent conversion assumptions.

Risk and claimant must also match: operating free cash flow belongs with an operating-capital discount rate, while equity cash flow belongs with cost of equity. Consistency does not mean every project deserves the company's average rate.

types.name: Frequency match
types.explanation: Periodic rate corresponds to payment dates.

types.name: Claimant match
types.explanation: Rate fits who receives the cash flow.

workedCase.setup: Assume an effective annual discount rate of 12% and a ₹100 payment in one month.
steps: Using 12% for that single month would give ₹89.29 and over-discount the payment.
workedCase.result: The annual label cannot be used as a monthly rate.
workedCase.interpretation: Using 12%/12 is exact only for the appropriate nominal quotation convention, not this effective annual rate.

analysis: Check units and payment dates.
Match currency and inflation conventions.
Match cash-flow ownership and risk to the rate.

explanation: The time value of money converts dated amounts to a common valuation date. Compounding moves an amount forward, while discounting moves it back. The rate must match the payment frequency, currency, inflation basis and risk. A 12% nominal annual quote compounded monthly differs from a 12% annual effective return.

Timelines prevent mistakes about annuities due, terminal values and loan balances. An instalment contains interest and principal; the principal component changes the balance on which later interest is charged. Project return measures also depend on all dated contributions and withdrawals rather than only the final amount.

types.name: Annuity
types.explanation: Equal periodic payments, with beginning- or end-period timing.

types.name: Growing or uneven stream
types.explanation: Payments change over time and require suitable formulas or individual discounting.

types.name: Perpetuity
types.explanation: A stream continuing indefinitely under restrictive sustainability assumptions.

workedCase.setup: You receive ₹110 at the end of year one and ₹121 at the end of year two. The relevant annual effective rate is 10%.
workedCase.result: The ₹231 nominal total is worth ₹200 at the selected date and rate.
workedCase.interpretation: A currency amount can be added directly only after its date and economic basis match. Present values depend on the required rate, not a desire for a particular answer.

analysis: Draw the dates and signs first.
Convert quoted rates to matching period rates.
Discount each claim consistently before aggregating it.
